components.text: Whether widespread belief in meaningful agency is behaviorally necessary for a functional society.
The decisive agency demand is defeated if neither material nor immaterial mentality can make libertarian choice intelligible.
The separate claim that agency-belief improves social functioning is not established or directly rebutted by the dilemma.
Why a deciding self escapes the exhaustive choice between prior determination and undetermined randomness.
The decisive demand is to explain how a deciding self escapes the determined-or-random dilemma.
The separate social-function issue is contacted by insisting that society needs belief in morally significant decisions.
The combination of possible free-will falsity and claimed social necessity for belief in morally weighty choice.
The claim that functional civilization needs widespread belief that free choice matters.
The decisive conditional is accepted arguendo and reversed: if false free will is socially necessary, that belief is the delusion.
The earlier claim that free-will belief is socially useful is conditionally accepted rather than independently challenged.
Whether divine authority uniquely compounds human fallibility by placing mistaken moral commands beyond correction.
The decisive authority concern is answered by arguing that transpersonal absolutes restrain self-interest and enable equal law.
The conditional risk that an erroneous divine attribution becomes immune to correction is not directly resolved.
Whether placing fundamental moral rules beyond ordinary dispute reliably restrains self-interest and supports social cohesion.
The decisive institutional claim is answered by showing that placing norms beyond debate protects harmful principles with the same force.
The asserted benefits of cohesion and restraint are expressly conceded as possible parts of the tradeoff.
Whether religious tradition should receive credit for universal moral and institutional advances attributed to its authoritative principles.
The inherited-religious-credit claim is challenged by asking whether advances arose against scripture and religious institutions.
Whether insulating fundamental norms from debate creates an unacceptable risk that harmful religious imperatives become similarly protected.
The decisive revisability challenge is answered by insisting that any durable society must place some moral commitments beyond ordinary contestation.
The historical claim that religious resistance obstructed particular advances is not directly contacted.
Whether scientific progress arose from religious intellectual foundations or instead through resistance to religious doctrines and institutions.
The decisive historical-credit challenge is answered by distinguishing motivating religious assumptions from later institutional resistance.
The broader danger that authoritative religion can protect harmful or mistaken positions is not directly resolved.
Whether religious assumptions should be credited as foundations of scientific inquiry despite religious suppression of scientific conclusions.
The decisive religious-support claim is answered with a documented-type counterexample in which scriptural authority expressly suppressed a scientific conclusion.
The move also illustrates the risk of treating authoritative norms as beyond challenge, though it does not address society's need for foundational commitments.
Whether scriptural authority's historical harms discredit the broader claim that religious interpretation can support human moral and rational development.
The broader demand about harmful scriptural authority is answered by distinguishing timeless endorsement from historically accommodated regulation and gradual humanization.
The specific Galileo suppression case is not directly answered by the slavery-accommodation distinction.
Whether historical accommodation explains scripture regulating slavery instead of prohibiting it while still reflecting a reforming divine morality.
The decisive accommodation claim is challenged by contrasting total bans on other entrenched practices with affirmative permissions concerning slavery and captives.
Why scripture permits severe slavery practices despite being able to prohibit other entrenched conduct and offer feasible reforms.
The decisive scriptural-direction challenge is answered by identifying universal dignity and duties to strangers as rival biblical principles supporting reform.
The specific question why severe permissions and feasible immediate reforms were omitted remains unanswered.
Whether gradual reform and universal biblical principles adequately reconcile concrete slavery rules with a humanizing moral trajectory.
Whether social feasibility prevented revelation from imposing materially more humane slavery rules.
The decisive gradual-reform claim is tested with a modest family-release rule that would reduce harm without requiring immediate universal abolition.
The earlier necessity of accommodation is directly challenged by presenting a feasible, socially bounded amelioration.
Whether religion's alleged social necessity gives a convinced atheist a truthful and practicable reason to adopt or transmit religious belief.
Whether the practical benefit of an agency-supporting religious belief can justify reliance on that belief if considered false.
The decisive practical conclusion is answered by separating conceded social benefit from the involuntary character of sincere belief.
The move does not address the prior scriptural or abolitionist claims.
How a convinced atheist can respond honestly if religious institutions are socially beneficial but their central claims remain unbelievable.
Whether religious institutional benefits answer the specific omitted family-release reform in scriptural slavery law.
The decisive honesty concern is answered in part by allowing doubt and presentation of competing views rather than requiring fabricated certainty.
The inability of a convinced atheist to choose sincere God-belief remains unresolved.
The concrete scriptural family-release counterexample is not addressed.
